outcome: Nothing since 26 January 2024 has bearing on whether infinitely many Euclid primes (primes of the form p_n# + 1) exist. In the window, PrimeGrid proved five new such primes (the largest, 9562633# + 1, submitted to PrimePages 29 June 2025), each adding one more instance; three new primes of the minus form p_n# - 1 were also found, which belong to the separate Kummer-prime bullet. Neither Wikipedia's Euclid number article (last revised 9 November 2025) nor its Primorial prime article (last edited 29 November 2025) reports any proof, and both still list the question as open.
problem_asks: Are there infinitely many Euclid primes? Read from the statement and the linked article (Euclid number): Euclid numbers are E_n = p_n# + 1, where p_n# is the product of the first n primes; a Euclid prime is an E_n that is prime (equivalently, a prime of the form p_n# + 1; the article calls these prime Euclid numbers or primorial primes). The bullet asks one thing: whether the set of n (or of such primes) is infinite. It does not ask (a) whether infinitely many E_n are composite, (b) anything about the minus form p_n# - 1 (Euclid number of the second kind / Kummer number), which the Wikipedia list gives as a separate bullet ('Kummer primes'), or (c) the Euclid-Mullin sequence, also a separate bullet.

events.what_happened: Caldwell and Gallot, 'On the primality of n! ± 1 and 2 × 3 × 5 × ... × p ± 1', Mathematics of Computation 71 (2002), no. 237, pp. 441–448. Per the Prime Pages reference note (opened), the paper extended the computed range for primality of p# ± 1, reported new primes (6380!+1, 6917!-1, and 42209#+1), and gave heuristic estimates of the expected number of such primes compared with the number found. The date is the journal year; the first public version may be earlier and was not checked.
events.delivers: A computed range of p# ± 1 primality plus heuristic expected-count estimates. Proves nothing about infinitude; the heuristic expects growth in the count, which is a conjecture, not a result.
events.remains: Whether infinitely many p_n# + 1 are prime (the whole question).

events.what_happened: Turker Ozsari, 'Claims On Primorial Primes', arXiv math/0310412 (v1 27 October 2003). The abstract says only that the note gives 'some claims on primorial prime numbers'. Reading the body through ar5iv (opened), it lists five numbered claims: Claim 2.1 'There are infinitely many plus-primorial prime numbers'; Claim 2.2 the same for minus-primorial primes; Claim 2.3 'infinitely many prime numbers which are neither'; Claims 2.4 and 2.5 about primes lying between consecutive primorial primes. The only proof visible in the extraction is of Proposition 1.7 (no prime is both plus- and minus-primorial). No proof of Claim 2.1 appears in what I could read.
events.revisions: v1 27 Oct 2003 only, as far as the abstract page shows.
events.delivers: Asserts, without visible proof, the answer 'yes' to the bullet's question (Claim 2.1). Establishes nothing: no argument for infinitude was found in the text read.
events.remains: Whether infinitely many p_n# + 1 are prime (the whole question), as far as the text read shows.
events.doubts: The claims are stated without proof in the extracted text. The only visible proof is of an unrelated proposition. Later sources (Wikipedia Euclid number, rev. 9 Nov 2025; Primorial prime, rev. 29 Nov 2025) still list the question open, so the note has not been taken up as a result. The search runs found no rebuttal or citation, but I did not search exhaustively for either. The full body was read only through the ar5iv rendering and may be incomplete.
events.direction: Asserts the conjecture (yes, infinitely many plus-primorial primes), without proof.

events.what_happened: George Lillie, 'About the Primality of Primorials', arXiv 2110.04302 (v1 10 October 2021). Per the abstract (opened), it gives probabilistic estimates: the probability that p_n# - 1 or p_n# + 1 is prime is O(1/n); that both are prime is O(1/n^2); it suggests there are in total about three instances where both are prime. A search snippet of the text also reports that the paper argues the e^gamma constant in the Caldwell–Gallot-type expected count should be revised to a constant in [1,2]; I did not open the full text to confirm that.
events.delivers: Heuristic probability estimates. Asserts no proof that either family is infinite. It bears on the joint (both-prime) question, which the bullet does not ask.
events.remains: Whether infinitely many p_n# + 1 are prime (the whole question).
events.doubts: Heuristic by its own description (probabilistic). Not a proof and not presented as one in the abstract.
events.direction: Heuristic evidence about frequency; neutral on whether the plus-form set is infinite.

disputes.summary: Prime Pages' Top 20 primorial table dates 42209# + 1 to May 1999 (proof code p8), but the Prime Pages reference note for Caldwell and Gallot (2002) says they found 42209#+1. Not resolved here; the record does not depend on it.

summary: The bullet asks whether infinitely many primes of the form p_n# + 1 (Euclid primes, E_n = p_n# + 1 prime) exist. Wikipedia's Euclid number article (opened; last revised 9 November 2025) defines them and lists the question as unsolved, calling the primes 'prime Euclid numbers (primorial primes)'; its Primorial prime article (opened; last edited 29 November 2025) says it is not known whether there are infinitely many, with the infobox listing the conjectured count as infinite. The largest known plus-form prime is 9562633# + 1 (n = 637,491), per both articles and OEIS A014545 (opened). In the window, PrimeGrid proved five new plus-form primes (4328927#+1 on 27 July 2024 discovery; 5256037#+1 on 6 August 2024; 6369619#+1 on 12 August 2024; 7351117#+1 submitted 20 September 2024; 9562633#+1 submitted 29 June 2025). Each is a computer-found explicit number, checked by PFGW N-1 tests, and each adds one instance without moving the infinitude question: under the scope test in §2.1, finitely many new instances of an existential-infinite question are not progress on it. Three minus-form primes were found in the same window (4778027#-1, 6354977#-1, 6533299#-1); they are recorded as discounted because the minus form is the separate Kummer-prime bullet. Two other in-window items are discounted as neighbouring questions: the Booker–Simon Euclid-Mullin generalisation (arXiv 2601.21901, 29 Jan 2026) and the compositorial record 751882!/751879#+1 (announced 28 Dec 2025). The only other infinitude claim I found is Ozsari's 2003 note 'Claims On Primorial Primes' (arXiv math/0310412), which asserts infinitely many plus-primorial primes (Claim 2.1) without a visible proof; no later source I opened accepts it, and Wikipedia still lists the question open. Heuristics (Caldwell–Gallot 2002, Lillie 2021) expect growth or give probabilistic estimates but prove nothing. Human checking of the record primes is limited to PrimePages' status conventions and PrimeGrid's own second-machine PFGW confirmation; no human written verification of any infinitude argument exists in what I found. AI: 34 searches (listed below) and the opened sources name no AI system for any Euclid or primorial prime event. The PrimeGrid search software (PRST, PFGW, MultiSieve, OpenPFGW) is computational, not AI. Two AI-adjacent leads were checked and do not connect to this problem: a June 2026 'Google DeepMind AI discovered a mathematical pattern hidden in prime numbers' item (lifeboat.com, 17 June 2026) has no primary source and does not mention primorials; and a 2026 Rochester talk ('Three big theorems about prime numbers') has an 'An AI breakthrough' heading whose content could not be read. Also, the t5k top-20 page and OEIS A005234 credit the plus-form records to PrimeGrid participants and to OEIS contributor Jeppe Stig Nielsen, who extended the OEIS list and is not credited with any proof.
competing_reading: One could read 'moved' broadly: the set of known Euclid primes grew by five in the window, and 9562633#+1 is a new largest. But the bullet asks only about infinitude and names no quantity (no count up to x, no bound) that these records move; each record is one more instance of the object the question is about. The record counts are consistent with the Caldwell–Gallot-type heuristic that expects roughly e^gamma log N primes up to N, which grows without bound and so fits the conjecture; nothing in the window makes the heuristic's expectation fail. No reading makes the window events a resolution.
what_would_settle_it: A proof that infinitely many n have p_n# + 1 prime (an arXiv or journal paper, or a Wikipedia/Prime Pages change to the status), or a proof that only finitely many do. A proof of either kind would appear as a new event; none was found through 10 October 2026 in the sources read. A second route is an explicit, checked statement in the literature (for instance a survey or problem database) that the question is still open as of 2026; the Wikipedia articles say so as of late 2025.

events.credibility_reason: Asserts infinitude (Claim 2.1) with no visible proof; no uptake in about 23 years on a landmark question; later sources (Wikipedia, Nov 2025) still list it open; labelled as 'claims' by its own title.

judgement.why: The statement asks only whether infinitely many p_n#+1 are prime. Each newly proved plus-form prime is one more finite instance (F5), so those events are instances, with direction null and no object role: a single prime is not what the statement asks for and does not contradict it. Minus-form primes belong to the separate Kummer-prime question, and the Booker–Simon paper and the compositorial record are about neighbouring questions, so all of these are variant. Lillie's heuristic settles nothing and is none. Ozsari's 2003 note asserts the answer without a visible proof and has had no uptake in 23 years, so it is none and not_credible. Nothing after the snapshot moves the question, and no AI involvement was found anywhere.
judgement.doubts: Verification for the record primes is marked checkable because each is an explicit number that a standard prover can re-test, though a re-test takes days of computing. This does not affect the outcome, since instances are discarded either way.
